task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: causal inference of next-possession PPP on AVOID labels
measurement reliability of PPP and labeling
confounding by team quality and game context

historical_evidence.finding: Cross‑possession memory of play‑type actions disappears after within‑team demeaning; apparent lag effects are confounded by team quality.
Global lag lifts for several play types collapse to zero within‑team; only SPOT_UP shows a weak lag‑1 effect. No persistent cross‑possession effect after controlling for team quality.
Descriptive net‑swing analysis of own PPP minus opponent next‑PPP; no formal test of effect on labeling.
No durable pivot branches or net‑swing effects across 52 playoff series; net swing negative for DRIVE/POST_UP but null for other play types.

failed_approaches.what_failed: attempt to detect decaying cross‑possession memory
failed_approaches.why: artifact from construction/selection bias; effect disappears after within‑team demeaning.

failed_approaches.what_failed: global lag analysis of play‑type impact
failed_approaches.why: artifact due to confounding; global lifts vanish after demeaning.
adequately powered null result; no durable effects found.

evidence_establishes: Cross‑possession memory of play‑type actions is negligible after adjusting for team quality.
No durable net‑swing effect of own PPP minus opponent next‑PPP across playoff series.
Negative net swing observed for DRIVE/POST_UP, suggesting opponent next‑PPP may reduce own scoring advantage.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether opponent next‑PPP drives AVOID labels for play X.
Whether own‑sequence lag effects influence AVOID labeling beyond simple cross‑possession memory.
uncertainties: Potential differences in labeling methodology across seasons; possibility of unmeasured context variables (e.g., defensive pressure, fatigue).

historical_effect.explanation: Historical evidence indicates that after controlling for team quality the cross‑possession effect is absent, but it does not preclude a subtle causal relationship. Therefore the decision remains to proceed with methodological refinements rather than abandon the question.

blocking_constraints.text: Team quality and game context may confound the relationship between opponent next‑PPP and AVOID labeling.
Teams may choose play X strategically when opponent next‑PPP is high or low, biasing estimates.
Reliability of PPP calculations and labeling consistency across seasons.
Testing multiple play types and lag orders increases false‑positive risk.

prior_work.summary: Prior studies found no persistent cross‑possession memory after within‑team demeaning, and no durable net‑swing effects across playoff series. These results suggest the effect, if any, is weak or confounded.

risks.text: Team performance, score margin, and defensive matchups may bias the apparent effect of opponent next‑PPP.
Strategic play‑choice may correlate with opponent next‑PPP.
PPP and labeling accuracy may vary across seasons.
Testing many play types and lag structures inflates type‑I error.

design.estimand: Causal effect of opponent next‑possession PPP on the probability of an AVOID label for play X (adjusted for within‑team baseline).
design.unit: Individual possession where play X is executed.
design.sample: All possessions in NBA 2022‑23 through 2025‑26 seasons where play X occurs (n≈200,000+).
design.power: With effect size |β|≈0.02 on probability scale and standard error ≈0.005, power >0.90 at α=0.05 (after Bonferroni).
design.controls: Team fixed effects, opponent fixed effects, score margin, period, game context, lag of own PPP, lag of opponent PPP, within‑team demeaning of PPP. Propensity‑score weighting to balance covariates across high vs low opponent PPP bins.
design.falsification: Apply the same model to a play type known not to be influenced by opponent PPP (e.g., free‑throw attempts) and expect no effect.
design.multiplicity: Bonferroni correction for 5 play types and 5 lag orders (α=0.05/25).
design.decision_rule: Reject null if p<α/25 for the main effect of opponent PPP; otherwise conclude no evidence of effect.
design.data_version: NBA 2022‑23 through 2025‑26 per‑game play‑by‑play and derived possession records.
